_meta.title: Base morphemes and affixes
_meta.description: A finite, teachable inventory of base words/roots and affixes used to place morpheme boundaries (which are hard syllable boundaries). This is the 'Option B' inventory that resolves the from-letters residue: farmer=farm+er because 'farm' is a listed base, while corner is NOT split as corn+er because it is not treated as a productive derivation of a listed base.
_meta.source_notes: Morphology as a distinct instructional layer, taught after core GPC/syllable work: UFLI Foundations; Wilson Reading System. Morphemes hold stable spelling across pronunciation shifts: Venezky (1970, 1999). '-ed' three-pronunciation rule and final-stable-syllable suffixes: Orton-Gillingham tradition.
_meta.status: seed — a small correct starting set; expand toward the common base-morpheme inventory taught in grades K-5

combiningForms._note: Neoclassical combining forms, from Greek and Latin. They belong in neither existing list: not `bases`, because they are not free words (there is no word 'therm'), and not `prefixes`, because prefixes attach to a free base while these combine with EACH OTHER - hypo+therm+ic has no free word anywhere in it. This is the layer that connects concepts rather than parses sentences: hypothermic and hyperthermic share `therm` and contrast only on hypo/hyper, and a learner who owns those three morphemes owns both words plus thermometer, thermal and isotherm.
combiningForms._position: Position is not free. An initial form precedes a final one, and most are fixed to one slot: photo- and hypo- are initial, -logy and -meter final, while therm and graph occur in both. Recorded per entry rather than assumed, because a parser that tries every form in every slot will split words that should stay whole.
combiningForms._self_example: The term for this category is itself one: neo-classic-al. `neo` is an initial combining form, `-ic` and `-al` are Class I suffixes stacking inside any Class II suffix that follows. A learner who owns neo, classic, -ic and -al owns the word that names the phenomenon.

derivational.gloss: relating to / having the nature of

inflectional.rule: /əd/ after t or d (adds a syllable); /d/ after a voiced sound; /t/ after a voiceless sound
after a sibilant (s, x, z, ch, sh)

suffixes._level_note: `level` records the Class I / Class II distinction (Siegel 1974; Kiparsky 1982). Class I suffixes (-ic, -al, -ity, -ous) attach CLOSER to the root and can shift stress; Class II (-ly, -ness, -ful, -less) attach outside them and leave stress alone. That ordering is why hypothermically is therm+ic+al+ly and never therm+ly+ic+al. Treat it as a strong tendency, not a law: Fabb (1988) showed level ordering overpredicts, and Hay & Plag (2004) replace it with complexity-based ordering, where a suffix that is easier to parse out attaches outside one that is harder - gradient, and computable from a corpus.

bases._note: Free base words a young reader is taught to recognize. Listing a form here authorizes morpheme splits like <base>+<suffix>. Deliberately conservative: absence of a base means look-alikes (corner, sister) stay with the phonological engine rather than being force-split.

residue._note: The irreducible memorize-list (heart words): words the simple productive rules cannot resolve from letters alone. Consulted by the engine BEFORE applying an ambiguous rule, so the RULE stays one sentence and these stay a plain list — not rule clauses.

edNotSuffix._rule: In these words the final 'ed' is NOT the non-syllabic -ed suffix; the 'e' is a real vowel and its own syllable (hun-dred, sa-cred, na-ked). Skip the -ed rule for them. They are unresolvable from letters (naked vs baked, jagged vs jogged).
